items.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001
items.q: I heard Miles with, I think, Cannonball and Coltrane... I was still trying to sort out the difference between the sound of a tenor and an alto

ctx.x: I’m sorry, that’s my nickname. You can’t—

Well I guess it is at that. But I used to, when I was in high school, I was right outside Washington where the Howard Theatre is. And I used to tell my mother and father, “I’m going to the theater tonight.” They thought I was going to go see a Roy Rogers thing. I’d © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

probably go to hear Shorty Rogers or somebody. I heard Nancy Wilson when she was maybe 21, right after she had done the two Capitol albums. And she was eight feet tall and weighed a hundred and fifteen pounds and pure dynamite in a floor length blue dress. And the curtain opened and the audience went [gasp], and she slayed them. And I heard Redd Foxx, I heard Moms Mabley, I heard Quincy Jones’ big band, I heard Miles with, I think, Cannonball and Coltrane and I’m pretty sure Bill Evans but my memory of the…

items.title: Frank Tate interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001
items.q: I don’t hear a lot of new, I mean we’re fresh out of Charlie Parkers and Coltranes.

ctx.x: Right. When you look at the audience.

Yeah well it’s the audience. And my late brother died a couple of years ago would be at 60 or 61 now, and he died a couple of years ago. He rode around in his car listening to 50s R&B. People 55 years old now talk about Grand Funk Railroad or whoever. They don’t know. People crowding 60 have had no exposure to this music. They don’t know beans about it. And that really doesn’t bode very well for us, but now modern music with this post-Wynton Marsalis invasion — it’s not an invasion it’s just people have gotten…
You don’t want to hear jazz and Irish reels together.
